name: simulation-core-contract
title: The simulation-core contract — model in, results + verification out
lead:
One function is the whole surface. `from viva_simulation_core import simulate`, or
`viva-sim simulate <model>`. You pass a model in any accepted form, choose the engine
(or a second engine to cross-check against), and get a SimulationResult carrying the
results and a VerificationReport. The engine is a box behind the contract — Tellurium
(roadrunner) is the main exact-SBML engine, COPASI a second — and the verification
reuses the core's own checks (finiteness, admissibility bounds, cross-engine
agreement), so every simulation ships with its own evidence instead of a bare
trajectory.

at_a_glance.role: THE CONTRACT — simulate(model, request) → results + verification, across model forms and engines, each run self-verified.

how_to_read:
The contract is one call: simulate(model, request) -> SimulationResult. `model` is an
SBML/Antimony string or file, or a dotted registered-composite id. `request` sets the
duration, interval, observables, engine, and an optional second engine to cross-check
against. The result carries `results` (observables over time) and `verification` (a
report with ran / finite / admissible-per-observable / optional cross-engine
agreement, and one `passed` verdict). Same interface, any model, any engine.
question:
What is the simulation core, in one interface? Can you hand it any model, ask it to
run under any engine, and get back both the results AND a verification that the run
can be trusted — through one common entry point, with no re-wrapping per caller?
hypothesis:
The simulation core is a single contract: simulate(model, request) -> results +
verification. A model (SBML/Antimony or a registered composite) goes in; the core
runs it under a swappable engine and returns the observables together with a
structured verification (ran, finite, physically admissible, and — on request —
cross-engine agreement).

executive.what_is_this:
The simulation core reduced to its contract. Where the companion investigation
(biogears-sbml-sepsis) demonstrates the core's capabilities one by one, this one
shows the single interface they all sit behind: simulate(model, request) -> results
+ verification. Study 00 runs several models through that one interface — an SBML
file under Tellurium, the same model cross-checked against COPASI, a different
engine, and a registered composite — and shows each returns results plus a passing
verification.
executive.verdict:
The simulation core is one interface: model in, results + verification out. The same
simulate() call runs an SBML file, the same model under a second engine, and a
registered composite, and each run returns its observables together with a structured
verification — ran, finite, admissible, and (when asked) cross-engine agreement
(Tellurium and COPASI agree to ~1e-4). The engine is swappable behind the contract,
and no simulator is wrapped more than once.
decisions_needed: Model intake: let simulate() also accept a pre-compiled / in-memory model handle, not only SBML text or a composite id, so a caller can re-run many models without re-parsing each one — a performance path on top of the same contract.

studies.name: 00-contract
studies.title: The contract — simulate(model, request) → results + verification
studies.question:
Can one interface take any model, run it under any engine, and return both the results
and a verification that the run can be trusted?

findings.summary: Four model/engine combinations run through one simulate() call, each returning results + a passing verification (chart 01).
findings.detail:
run_contract.py drives four runs through the single interface
simulate(model, request) (out/contract_runs.json, chart 01):
  * an SBML file under Tellurium (roadrunner/CVODE);
  * the same SBML file with a cross-engine check against COPASI;
  * the same SBML file under COPASI directly;
  * a registered composite id with a severity override.
Each returns a SimulationResult: the requested observables over time, plus a
VerificationReport. All four verify (ran, finite, physically admissible on every
observable). The model form (file vs composite) and the engine (Tellurium vs COPASI)
change behind the interface; the call, the result shape, and the verification are the
same. The simulation core made concrete: one entry point, any model, any engine,
no per-caller re-wrapping.

findings.summary: Verification is a first-class output: ran / finite / admissible / cross-engine, with Tellurium and COPASI agreeing to ~1e-4.
findings.detail:
The contract returns evidence, not just a trajectory. The VerificationReport carries
ran and finite (no NaN/inf), physical admissibility per observable (e.g. MAP and SVR
positive, tissue integrity in [0,1]), and — when a second engine is named — the
cross-engine agreement. On the cross-checked run, Tellurium and COPASI (two
independent exact-SBML integrators) agree to a maximum relative difference of ~1e-4
across the observables, so the run passes the cross-engine gate. The verification
layer is the same set of checks developed across the companion investigation
(finiteness, admissibility bounds from study 04, cross-engine agreement from the
COPASI arm), now returned automatically with every simulation. A unit check confirms
the gate bites: a run with a negative MAP or a NaN fails verification.
findings.statement: The simulation core's value is one interface plus built-in verification — results you can trust, with the engine swappable behind the contract.
findings.explanation: The point of the contract is that the two outputs travel together. A caller hands a model to simulate() and gets back results and a verdict on whether to trust them, without knowing or managing which engine ran it. The engine behind the contract is a box: Tellurium is the main exact-SBML engine, COPASI a second, and a cross-engine run is itself a verification primitive (two independent integrators agreeing to ~1e-4 is evidence the result is engine-independent). The honest limit, and the next step, is the model intake: today simulate() accepts SBML text or a composite, which the engine parses; letting it also accept a pre-compiled / in-memory model handle would let a caller re-run many models without re-parsing each one. The contract is in place; widening its model intake is the forward work.

studies.claim:
simulate(model, request) is the simulation core's one interface: model in, results +
verification out. Four runs through the identical call (run_contract.py ->
out/contract_runs.json, chart 01) each return their observables together with a
VerificationReport — ran, finite, physical admissibility per observable, and, when a
second engine is requested, cross-engine agreement. The SBML file runs under Tellurium
and under COPASI; the same model cross-checked against COPASI agrees with Tellurium to
~1e-4; a registered composite runs through the same interface with a severity override.
Every run is self-verified; the engine is a swappable box behind the contract, and no
simulator is wrapped more than once.

derived.insight: Four model/engine combinations run through one simulate() call, each returning results + a passing verification (chart 01).
